Totally
TOH-tuh-lee
adverb / interjection (Gen X slang)
From total (Latin totus, whole) + -ly; in standard English since the 1500s for "wholly, completely." As a free-standing intensifier and one-word assent ("Totally!") it was the signature adverb of the early-1980s Valley Girl dialect of the San Fernando Valley, fixed in national memory by Frank and Moon Unit Zappa’s single "Valley Girl" (1982) and the film Valley Girl (1983); "totally tubular," "totally awesome," and "totally rad" followed through the decade, and Totally survives in Millennial clipped form as totes.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

In Gen X speech totally stopped meaning wholly and started meaning very, then yes: "That’s totally awesome." "Are you coming?" "Totally." The word that once measured completeness became a vocal shrug of enthusiasm, attached to a pizza, a sweater, or a weekend plan with exactly the same force. The Christian observation is that the old meaning was too good to waste. Scripture asks for one thing totally and only one: "thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might" (Deu 6:5). Blessed are they "that seek him with the whole heart" (Psa 119:2), and the apostle prays that God would "sanctify you wholly" — spirit, soul, and body (1Th 5:23). When everything is totally something, nothing is wholly anything; the intensifier spends the coin that should have been saved for God. The same Lord who wants the whole heart also wants plain speech: "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay" (Mat 5:37). A father can let his son say totally about a ball game; he should teach him there is only one place the word is fully true — a heart given over entirely to Christ, who gave Himself entirely for it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen X / Valley Girl intensifier and one-word assent ("Totally!") — the adverb of wholeness flattened into "very" and "yes"; Scripture keeps wholly for the love of God with all the heart (Deu 6:5).

expand to see more

TOTALLY, adv. and interj. (Gen X slang, early 1980s, San Fernando Valley) Very, extremely; as a stand-alone reply, "yes, absolutely." "That party was totally awesome." "Totally!"

Stock compounds: totally tubular, totally rad, totally awesome, totally grody; delivered with rising Valley intonation.

Later forms: Millennial totes; the word is still the default emphatic in American teen speech forty years on.

Webster 1828: TOTALLY, adv. Wholly; entirely; fully; completely; as, to be totally exhausted; all hope totally failed; he was totally absorbed in thought.

Decode for parents: when every opinion is held "totally," children lose the vocabulary for the one devotion God asks to be whole.

Key Scripture

Deu 6:5 — "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might."

Psa 119:2 — "Blessed are they that keep his testimonies, and that seek him with the whole heart."

1Th 5:23 — "And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ."

Mat 5:37 — "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil."

Jas 5:12 — "But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation."

Modern Corruption

Totally spends the word for wholeness on sweaters and pizza; Scripture keeps it for the one devotion God asks to be entire — all the heart, all the soul, all the might.

expand to see more

Inflation of the superlatives. A generation that called everything totally something trained its ear to hear whole-hearted language as noise. The same thing has happened to awesome, amazing, and literally: the strongest words in the language become filler, and when a man finally needs to say that something is wholly true — a vow, a confession, a promise to his wife — the words have already been spent. Our Lord’s rule for speech is not a ban on enthusiasm but a demand that words carry their weight: Yea, yea; Nay, nay (Mat 5:37).

The word worth recovering. The Shema is the original "totally": all thine heart, all thy soul, all thy might (Deu 6:5). The Psalmist blesses the man who seeks God "with the whole heart" (Psa 119:2), and Paul prays that God would sanctify believers "wholly" (1Th 5:23). The Christian does not need to stop saying totally; he needs to know what the word is for, and to give it there first.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin totus (whole) → English total, totally (wholly) → early-1980s Valley Girl intensifier and one-word assent → Millennial totes.

Latin totus — whole, entire, all

English total / totally (16th c.) — wholly, completely

Early 1980s San Fernando Valley: totally as all-purpose intensifier ("totally tubular")

1982 Zappa single "Valley Girl" and the 1983 film carry it nationwide

Millennial clipping totes; Scripture’s wholeness: all the heart (Deu 6:5)

Usage

""Are you going to the mall Saturday?" "Totally!""

"Everything was totally awesome in 1984; only one thing is asked of us wholly (Deu 6:5)."

"Seek Him with the whole heart (Psa 119:2) — the one place totally is literally true."
